explain: Offline writes rule out any model that needs a quorum, so linearizable and sequential are out. With replicas accepting writes independently, concurrent edits will conflict, and convergence requires a deterministic merge (a CRDT or last-writer-wins, which can drop data).

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Hot keys: perfect key balance, unbalanced traffic
question: A counter key receives 50,000 increments per second; a shard can absorb 8,000 writes per second. Which fix actually works?
options: Add more shards to the ring
Give the shard more virtual nodes
Split the counter into 10 sub-counters with suffixes and sum them on read
Put a client-side read cache in front of it
explain: A single key lives on one shard, so more shards or tokens cannot divide its traffic. A read cache does nothing for writes. Splitting into 10 sub-keys spreads about 5,000 writes per second to each (if they hash to different shards), and the price is that a read must fetch and add all 10.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Weighting soft scores with function_score and phased ranking
question: In our function_score query, what is the effect of `"boost_mode": "replace"`?
options: The final score is the combined function score; the wrapped query's score is ignored
The filters are replaced by the functions
Each function's weight replaces its own output
Missing fields are replaced by the origin
explain: boost_mode decides how the function result combines with the query score; replace uses only the function score. Here the wrapped query is filter-only and scores 0, so the default multiply would make every final score 0.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: SAT solvers: DPLL, unit propagation and clause learning
question: In the example, what makes x5 the first UIP of the conflict?
options: It was the first literal assigned at level 3
It is the only level-3 node that every path from the decision x3 to the conflict passes through, closest to the conflict
It appears in the most clauses of the formula
It has the highest VSIDS activity
explain: A unique implication point at the conflict level is a node every path from that level's decision to the conflict goes through. The decision x3 is always one; the first UIP is the one nearest the conflict, here x5. Cutting there gives (not x4 or not x5), which is shorter and more general than the decision-only clause.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: What ships in an image: base images, distroless and scanning
question: Your scanner reports no vulnerabilities for an image built last month. What should you conclude?
options: The image has no bugs
No currently published advisory matches a package the scanner recognised; rescan regularly because new CVEs are published every day
The image will stay clean
Scanning is unnecessary for this image
explain: A scan is a snapshot against today's databases and only covers packages it can identify. New advisories appear constantly, so running images need continuous rescanning.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: A hardened pod spec, line by line
question: Your cluster's kubelets run without seccompDefault. A pod spec sets no seccompProfile. Which seccomp profile does it get?
options: RuntimeDefault
Docker's default profile
Unconfined
Localhost
explain: The Kubernetes seccomp tutorial says pods use RuntimeDefault by default only when seccompDefault is enabled; otherwise the default is Unconfined. Set it in the pod or enable the kubelet option.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Pod Security Admission and policy engines
question: A namespace has `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted`. A user applies a Deployment whose pod template sets `privileged: true`. What happens?
options: The Deployment is accepted, but its pods are rejected when the ReplicaSet tries to create them
PSA mutates the template to remove privileged
The pods start but are killed after 60 seconds
The Deployment is rejected immediately
explain: The PSA docs state enforce applies only to the resulting pod objects, while audit and warn also apply to workload resources. PSA validates; it never mutates.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Escapes in the runtime: runc CVE-2019-5736 and Leaky Vessels
question: Which control blocked CVE-2019-5736 even on unpatched runc, according to the advisory?
options: Network policies
The default AppArmor profile
A read-only root filesystem
User namespaces where the host's root is not mapped into the container
explain: The advisory says it is not blocked by the default AppArmor policy but is blocked by correct use of user namespaces: container root is then not host root, so it cannot write the host runc binary.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: What an image actually is: layers, unions and digests
question: The last instruction in a build deletes a 300 MB cache directory that an earlier instruction created. What happens to the size of the pushed image?
options: It shrinks by 300 MB, because the final filesystem no longer contains the directory
The build fails, because whiteouts may not refer to lower layers
The earlier layer is rewritten without the directory
A new layer of whiteouts is added; the 300 MB stays in the earlier blob and is still pulled
explain: A removal is recorded as a whiteout in the new layer, and whiteouts only hide names in lower layers. The earlier blob is immutable and content addressed, so it still holds the bytes and is still downloaded. To avoid shipping them, create and delete within one layer, or build in one stage and copy only the output into a second.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: Autoscaling and GPU scheduling: two control loops
question: A Deployment runs 4 replicas, each container requesting 500m CPU. The HPA targets 50% average utilization and the pods average 400m. What does the controller write, and does it keep scaling?
options: 6 now, then 7 on the next tick
8, doubling because utilization is 80%
7, and it stops: at 7 replicas the ratio is 0.914, inside the default 0.1 tolerance
5, because the controller adds at most one replica per period
explain: The target per pod is 50% of the 500m request, so 250m. The ratio is 400 / 250 = 1.6 and the ceiling of 4 x 1.6 = 6.4 is 7. If total demand is unchanged, 7 pods average 1600 / 7 = 228.57m, a ratio of 0.914, which is 0.086 from 1.0 and inside the tolerance, so the loop settles. A later scale down would additionally wait out the 300 s stabilization window.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Resolving the second one and those against what was shown
question: Which use of *those* should become a filter edit rather than a frozen set of ids?
options: save those
email me those
only those that are remote
compare those
explain: *only those that are remote* narrows the search, and should keep working as postings change, so it is a constraint added to the filters. Saving, emailing and comparing act on the specific items on screen.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Hidden computation: filler tokens, encoded reasoning, paraphrasing
question: A team paraphrases its reasoning model's scratchpad paragraph by paragraph at inference time, and MATH accuracy drops 7%. What should they conclude?
options: Not much yet: unfamiliar-looking scratchpads can distract the model, so compare training on paraphrased versus original scratchpads before inferring encoding
The model uses encoded reasoning, since meaning was preserved and accuracy fell
The model uses filler-token computation
The paraphraser is too weak and must be replaced with a stronger model
explain: Anthropic found that merely splitting the scratchpad into blocks, with no paraphrasing, cut MATH pass@1 by 7%. A drop at inference time has innocent causes. Distilling paraphrased scratchpads into a model and comparing accuracy controls for that. A stronger paraphraser cannot be trusted not to share the code.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Why CoT is monitorable at all, and how to keep it so
question: Which misbehavior is a CoT monitor most likely to catch in a current reasoning model?
options: Choosing an answer because a metadata tag in the prompt says so
Agreeing with a user's stated opinion on a multiple-choice question
Reporting a slightly wrong number in a results table
Finding and exploiting a multi-step bug in a test harness that requires exploring several files
explain: The test-harness exploit needs exploration and planning, which must pass through the CoT, and Baker et al. caught such hacks at high rates. The other three can be done in a single forward pass (Chen et al.'s hints, Turpin's sycophancy) or need little reasoning (Emmons et al.'s example of faking a table entry), so silence is the default.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: Streams, the default stream trap, and events
question: You create four streams with cudaStreamCreate and issue, per chunk: H2D, kernel, D2H. Between chunk 1 and chunk 2 you add a cudaMemcpy (no stream) for a small constant buffer. What happens?
options: That copy is on the NULL stream, so it waits for all four blocking streams to drain and everything after it waits for the copy
Nothing changes; a small copy cannot affect scheduling
Only chunk 2's H2D is delayed, by the length of the small copy
The four streams keep overlapping but the results of chunk 1 become undefined
explain: The legacy default stream is a blocking stream: it waits for all other blocking streams, and they wait for it. Two operations from different streams cannot run concurrently if any NULL stream operation is submitted in between. The small copy becomes a full barrier. Creating the streams with cudaStreamNonBlocking, or compiling with --default-stream per-thread, removes it.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: CUDA Graphs: paying the launch cost once
question: Your decode step issues 180 kernels averaging 40 us each and you replay the step 2000 times. Launch overhead is about 0.9 us per kernel. Is a CUDA graph worth capturing?
options: Yes: 180 kernels is many small kernels, exactly the graph case
No: graphs only help when kernels are under 3 us
Yes: 360000 launches easily amortize the 400 us instantiation
Probably not much: overhead is about 2.2 percent of the step, so a graph can recover at most a fraction of that
explain: At 40 us per kernel, 0.9 us of overhead is 0.9/40.9 = 2.2 percent of wall time, and a graph removes only part of that (0.9 us to 0.5 us in the measured case), so the ceiling is roughly 1 percent. Amortization is fine and 180 kernels is a lot, but neither matters if the overhead being removed is tiny. Measure the fraction first.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: Host memory as a tier: unified memory, zero-copy and offloading
question: Prototype code uses cudaMallocManaged for a 10 GB input that each kernel streams through once. The profile shows many small GPU page faults and slow kernels. What is the first fix?
options: Switch the input to pageable malloc memory
Issue cudaMemPrefetchAsync for the next chunk on a stream before the kernel that needs it, so pages move in bulk ahead of use
Raise the kernel's block count so faults overlap better
Use a higher stream priority for the kernel
explain: On-demand faulting migrates pages one fault at a time while warps stall. A stream-ordered prefetch moves the data ahead of use and fits into the copy and compute pipeline of lesson 5, with the guide noting it completes before any later operation in that stream. Priorities and block counts do not remove the faults.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Inside the forward pass: query and document attend to each other
question: Why can a search engine cache document embeddings for a bi-encoder but not intermediate document states for a cross-encoder?
options: Cross-encoder hidden states are too large to store
In a cross-encoder every document token attends to the query tokens in every layer, so its states differ for each query
Cross-encoders use random dropout at inference time
Bi-encoders use a different tokenizer that is deterministic
explain: Attention mixes query tokens into each document token's representation from the first layer on. A cache keyed by document would be wrong for every new query. Size is a secondary issue; dropout (randomly zeroing some activations, used only as a training regularizer) is off at inference.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: What cryptography promises, and to whom
question: A web form sends a price to the server over an encrypted connection, and the server trusts that price. A user edits the price in their own browser before sending. Which goal failed?
options: None of the cryptographic goals: the sender is the attacker, so the server must not trust client-supplied data
Confidentiality: the encryption was too weak
Integrity: the ciphertext was altered in transit
Authenticity: the server did not know who sent it
explain: The connection did its job: nobody in the middle read or changed anything. The attacker is the legitimate endpoint. Cryptography protects data between parties; it cannot make an untrusted party honest. That is an access control and validation problem.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Block ciphers: what AES actually does to 16 bytes
question: How many bytes does AES encrypt in one call of the block function, whatever the key size?
options: Depends on the key size
explain: The AES block is always 128 bits, which is 16 bytes. Key size (128, 192 or 256 bits) only changes the key and the number of rounds.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: When hashes break: MD5, Flame and the SHA-1 collision
question: Why could Flame's authors reuse Microsoft's signature instead of forging one?
options: The signature covered an MD5 hash, and their malicious certificate had the same MD5 hash as one Microsoft did sign
They stole Microsoft's private key
Windows did not check signatures
MD5 is reversible
explain: Signatures sign hashes. A collision means two different inputs share the hash, so one signature validates both. No key was stolen.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Diffie-Hellman: agreeing on a secret in public
question: Eve recorded p = 23, g = 5, A = 8 and B = 19. What does Eve still lack to compute the shared secret directly?
options: Either secret exponent a or b (a discrete log)
Nothing, the secret is A x B mod p
The value of g
Bob's public key certificate
explain: The shared secret is g^(ab). From public values alone Eve needs a discrete log; at 23 that is a table lookup, at 2048 bits it is infeasible.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Sound primitives, broken systems: how crypto use fails
question: A code review finds `if request_sig == expected_sig:` in a webhook handler that uses HMAC-SHA-256. Which reviewer question does this line raise?
options: What must never repeat?
Is anything secret compared?
Where does randomness come from?
Is the key used for one purpose?
explain: The expected HMAC tag is secret until the attacker has it, and `==` may stop at the first differing byte, so response time can leak how much of a guess is right. Lesson 8 covers the fix, `hmac.compare_digest`. Nothing here repeats or draws randomness.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Nonce budgets for AEAD: counters, random nonces, XChaCha, GCM-SIV
question: A queue consumer encrypts messages with AES-GCM using `counter += 1` held in memory, starting at 0 each time the container starts. Containers are restarted on every deploy. What is wrong?
options: Each restart reuses nonces 0, 1, 2 and so on under the same key
Nothing: counters guarantee uniqueness
Counters are predictable, and GCM nonces must be secret
AES-GCM cannot use counter nonces
explain: GCM nonces only need to be unique, not secret or unpredictable, so a counter is fine in principle. The bug is that the counter resets while the key does not. Persist the counter (or reserve blocks of it), give each container a distinct fixed field, or use random nonces with a budget or a misuse-resistant AEAD.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Randomness in practice: weak, shared and first-boot keys
question: A company builds a golden virtual machine image with the SSH host key already generated, then clones it 500 times. What is the risk?
options: None, because SSH keys are 3072 bits long
All 500 servers share one private key, so stealing it from any one breaks all of them, and clients cannot tell the servers apart
The servers will refuse to start
Only the first clone can use the key
explain: A key in an image is copied, not regenerated. Every clone holds the same private key. Generate host keys on first boot (after the entropy pool is ready) and remove keys from images.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Reviewing crypto code: safe APIs, tests and migration
question: NIST IR 8547 deprecates RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography after 2030. What design property in your own message formats makes that migration easiest?
options: Hard-coding the algorithm in each function for speed
Using the longest available RSA keys
A version field and key id in every message, with the algorithm chosen in configuration
Encrypting everything twice
explain: Versioned formats with key ids let new and old algorithms coexist during migration and let you rotate keys without guessing which one made a message. Longer RSA keys do not resist a quantum attack.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: From MMA atoms to TiledMMA and TiledCopy
question: Why do GMMA atoms on Hopper give every thread the whole A tile in their A layout instead of splitting it across threads?
options: Because Hopper has no registers for operands
Because wgmma reads A and B from shared memory through a descriptor built on the whole tile
Because CuTe cannot partition across 128 threads
To make every thread load A from global memory
explain: The docs explain that the GMMA descriptor is built on the full A or B tile in shared memory, so the ALayout maps every thread to the same tile (stride 0 in the thread mode) and CuTe checks that the shared memory layout is valid for a descriptor.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: CXL protocols, device types and the path of one load
question: Which statement about a CPU write to CXL memory is correct?
options: The OS takes a page fault and copies the page to the device
The device DMA engine pulls the data from host memory
Writes must use special non-temporal instructions
The store goes into the CPU cache; when the dirty line is later evicted, the host sends an RwD and the device replies with an NDR
explain: CXL.mem is plain cache-coherent memory from the core's point of view. Stores land in the cache; the eviction of a dirty line becomes a request-with-data message, acknowledged by a no-data response.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Three questions before you touch a system: law, permission, ethics
question: A client signs a test agreement covering 'all our cloud servers'. One server in the list is actually run by a hosting company on shared hardware. What is the right move?
options: Test it: the client listed it, so it is in scope
Confirm ownership and get the hosting provider's terms or consent before testing anything that is not the client's to authorise
Test it gently, at night, so nobody notices
Skip the agreement and rely on the bug bounty rules of the hosting company
explain: Only someone entitled to control a system can authorise access to it. A client's list proves what the client believes, not what it owns. Many cloud providers publish their own testing policies; read them and keep the result with the agreement.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: The UK Computer Misuse Act, section by section
question: Under CMA section 5, which fact alone gives a section 1 offence a significant link to England and Wales?
options: The accused speaks English
The target server was in England at the time, even if the accused was abroad
The website uses a .uk domain name
The victim company is listed on the London Stock Exchange
explain: Section 5(2) gives two links for section 1: the accused was in the home country when acting, or the computer containing the targeted program or data was. A domain name or a listing is not on the list.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Export controls: Wassenaar and 'intrusion software'
question: A researcher in the US emails exploit details for a router bug to the router vendor's security team abroad, so they can fix it. Which concept in the 2021 BIS rule fits best?
options: Deemed export to an E:1 country
Vulnerability disclosure
Entity List designation
Intrusion software production
explain: The rule defines vulnerability disclosure as identifying, reporting or communicating a vulnerability to people responsible for remediating it, to resolve it. The 2017 Wassenaar change excluded such technology exchanges from the development-technology control.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Cover-ups and whistleblowing: Uber's CSO and Twitter's security lead
question: Why could Sullivan be convicted of misprision of a felony?
options: Because Uber's bug bounty programme was illegal
Because a security officer must publish every bug
Because the evidence showed the hackers committed a CFAA felony, Sullivan knew it, and took steps to conceal it instead of reporting it
Because the hackers were from another country
explain: The Ninth Circuit explained that misprision needs a completed felony by the principal (here unauthorised access under the CFAA), knowledge of it, and concealment. The NDA could not retroactively authorise the access.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: The domain-weight update, step by step
question: A colleague's DoReMi port returns the domain weights from the final step instead of the average over steps. What is the likely effect?
options: The output is noisier and reflects only the end of training, while the method (following Nemirovski et al.) returns the average over the trajectory
None, because the weights converge to a fixed point after a few steps
Weights will no longer sum to 1
The proxy model will diverge
explain: Per-step weights react to one minibatch and keep moving as the proxy learns. The paper returns the average over all T steps, which is smoother and integrates the whole run, including the early phase when weights change most.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Fitting a mixing law: RegMix, data mixing laws, judging a mixture
question: Your linear regression over 5 domains recommends putting 100 percent of the budget on Wikipedia. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Wikipedia really is the best data and the other domains add nothing
A linear function over mixtures always has its minimum at a corner, so the pick reflects the model's form, not the data
The regression has too many runs and is overfitting
The proxy models were too large
explain: A linear function on the probability simplex is minimized at a vertex, a single-domain mixture. Mixture effects are nonlinear (the first few percent of a domain matter most), which is why RegMix prefers LightGBM and averages the top 100 predicted mixtures.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Curation inside a domain: quality filters from phi-1 to FineWeb-Edu
question: Your GitHub domain is full of auto-generated config files. Which tool addresses this directly?
options: DoReMi, by lowering GitHub's domain weight
A document-level quality filter that drops low-value files inside the domain
Raising the smoothing parameter c
Iterated DoReMi with more rounds
explain: DoReMi can only scale the whole GitHub domain up or down, which also cuts the good code. Removing specific bad documents is a curation job, like phi-1's educational-value classifier.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Worked example: binary search over animation keyframes
question: A teammate measures one cold lookup and finds SoA only 16% faster, so they conclude the split is pointless. What is the strongest reply?
options: The measurement must be wrong; SoA is always 4x faster here
Per-lookup misses are similar, but the searched data is 4x smaller, so across many lookups it stays cached and the gap widens
SoA only helps with SIMD, and binary search is not vectorized
They should switch to a linked list of keyframes
explain: A single cold lookup misses in both layouts on its first few probes. The benefit of a 512-byte index over a 2 KiB one shows up when many lookups reuse the same lines, which is how an animation system runs.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Classification: levels, impact and the high-water mark
question: A system stores public product photos (confidentiality not applicable, integrity LOW, availability LOW) and customer support chats (confidentiality MODERATE, integrity LOW, availability LOW). What is its FIPS 199 confidentiality?
options: NOT APPLICABLE, because most of its data is public
LOW, the average
MODERATE, the highest value among its information types
HIGH, because it is customer-facing
explain: FIPS 199 uses the high-water mark: the system's value for each objective is the highest among its information types. Volume and averages do not matter; the support chats set confidentiality to MODERATE.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Tokens and masks: taking real values out of systems
question: An attacker steals the full orders database of a shop that uses vault tokenisation. What do they get for card numbers?
options: The card numbers, because the token is an encoding of them
Random tokens that only the vault can map back to card numbers
Card numbers, but only the last four digits
Encrypted card numbers they can brute-force offline
explain: Vault tokens are random and the mapping lives only in the vault, so there is nothing to decode or brute-force in the stolen table. Vaultless tokens (FPE, AES-SIV) are different: anyone with the key can reverse them.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Where DLP acts: endpoints, email, web and cloud
question: Why deploy a new DLP blocking rule in simulation mode first?
options: Simulation mode is faster
Because blocking rules are illegal in some countries
To measure how often it would fire and on what, and tune precision, before it blocks legitimate work
Simulation mode encrypts the data
explain: Simulation applies no actions but records matches, so you can measure false positives on real traffic and fix the detector or scope. Turning blocking on first usually breaks business processes and drives users to unmonitored channels.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a data security programme, and practice
question: Which pairing of case and missing control is right?
options: Tea 2025: no TLS on uploads
Snowflake 2024: no field-level encryption
OPM 2015: no data classification
Morgan Stanley: no per-device certificate review or serial reconciliation
explain: Morgan Stanley's failures were vendor oversight, unreviewed certificates and missing inventory. Tea's was retention not enforced; the Snowflake thefts used valid credentials without MFA or network allow lists; at OPM, officials said encryption would not have stopped attackers with valid credentials.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Honeytokens and canary tokens: data that phones home
question: A Word canary token sits on a file share. Which of these would NOT trigger it?
options: An intruder opening the file in Microsoft Word on Windows
A colleague opening it in Word on macOS
An intruder copying the file to their own machine and opening it there in Word while online
An intruder listing the share's file names without opening anything
explain: The Word token fires when Office opens the document and fetches its remote resource, wherever that happens. Listing names does not open the file. (A desktop.ini folder token is the type that fires on browsing.)

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Deception in Active Directory: honey accounts and honey SPNs
question: Which property should a honey account NOT have?
options: An attractive name such as SQL-Admin
A long random password
No legitimate use
Membership in a real privileged group so it looks authentic
explain: Real privileges turn the decoy into a real target. Make it look privileged (names, adminCount, fake groups) without granting anything.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Two orderings, two answers: float addition is not associative
question: A kernel sums 4096 float32 products. You pin the reduction so that every run uses the same tree in the same order. What have you guaranteed?
options: The result now equals the exact mathematical sum.
The same inputs give the same bits on every run of the same build and hardware, although the result is still not the exact sum.
The result is now within one ulp of the exact sum.
Any other implementation of the same sum will now agree with you bitwise.
explain: Fixing the order buys reproducibility, not accuracy. The rounding errors are still there; they are simply the same errors every time. A different kernel with a different tree is equally valid IEEE 754 and will generally give different bits.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Testing equivalence: bitwise, tolerance and the cache-hit test
question: A cached and an uncached run emit different token ids but detokenize to the same text. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The cache is broken and the test should fail.
The test should only ever compare at the text level, since text is what users receive.
Users are unaffected, but the numerics genuinely differ, so a logit-level or bitwise test is the one that will localize the cause.
The tokenizer is nondeterministic and should be reseeded.
explain: Identical text with different ids is possible, so text equality is the weakest of the three levels. It is the right contract to promise a user and the wrong instrument for finding the cause, which lives in the logits. Compare at the logit level to localize, then state the guarantee at the level you actually promise.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Knowing a run went wrong: invariants, oracles and liveness
question: Your DST suite injects only crashes that always restart within 2 simulated seconds and partitions that always heal within 5. Which bug is it most likely to miss?
options: Two leaders committing different values in the same term
A follower that never catches up while one peer stays permanently down
A torn write corrupting the log
An off-by-one in log index comparison
explain: That is a liveness bug, and it hides whenever faults heal on their own, exactly as in TigerBeetle's resonance bug. The other options are safety violations that can show up under transient faults. To catch liveness bugs, make some faults permanent and require a healthy quorum to keep making progress.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Runners: where pipeline code runs, and how to isolate it
question: A team runs self-hosted runners and adds a script that wipes and re-images each VM after a job finishes. GitHub's guidance says this is weaker than it looks. Why?
options: Re-imaging is too slow to matter
GitHub-hosted runners are never wiped either
Wiping removes the runner's registration token, which breaks the next job
Nothing guarantees the runner took only one job before the wipe, so a second job (possibly privileged) can still land on a dirty machine; JIT runners are registered for exactly one job
explain: The secure use reference says automatic destruction might not be as effective as intended because there is no way to guarantee a self-hosted runner only runs one job. A just-in-time runner is removed by GitHub after at most one job.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Caches and artifacts: how Ultralytics was poisoned
question: A pull_request_target workflow checks out PR code but has a read-only GITHUB_TOKEN and no secrets. Before GitHub's cache restrictions, what could still go wrong?
options: The PR code could use the job's cache token to write cache entries under main's scope, which a later release workflow would restore
Nothing: a read-only token cannot change anything
The PR could merge itself
The runner would crash
explain: This is exactly Adnan Khan's finding: the runtime cache token is separate from GITHUB_TOKEN. Writing into main's cache scope turned a low-privilege job into code inside the release.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Policy as code with OPA and Rego
question: In Rego, a rule body has five lines. Four are true for a resource and one is false. What happens?
options: The rule does not fire for that resource, because lines in a body are joined by AND
The rule fires, since most lines are true
Rego raises an error
The rule fires once for each true line
explain: All lines in a body must hold for the same choice of variables. To express OR, write a second rule with the same name.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a secure pipeline, a response plan, practice
question: Which of these is still a gap in the finished pipeline, and needs a different control?
options: A PR that edits the Makefile to steal secrets
An engineer opening a port in the console during an incident
A tampered pip cache restored by the release job
A wildcard OIDC trust on the apply role
explain: The first, third and fourth are handled inside the pipeline (no secrets on PRs, no release caches, an exact environment trust checked by policy). Console changes skip the pipeline; drift detection, and cloud guardrails that limit who may change security groups, are the controls for them.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Build it: turn your GPT into a masked diffusion LM
question: A learner trains the diffusion model but forgets change 3, keeping the AR loader whose targets are the inputs shifted by one. Attention is bidirectional. What does training do?
options: It works the same, since the shift does not matter
Wherever the next character is visible the model just copies it, so the loss falls without real learning, and outputs no longer predict their own positions as the sampler expects
Training fails with a shape error
It becomes an ordinary autoregressive model
explain: With full attention and a target of x[i+1] at position i, the answer sits in the input one position to the right whenever that position is visible. The model learns to copy its neighbour. Causal attention is what makes the shifted target a real prediction task. DiffuLLaMA's shift in lesson 8 is different: output i is scored only when position i+1 itself is masked, so nothing leaks.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Why prefill stalls decode on a shared GPU
question: Which metric does a chat user notice first if prefills are always scheduled ahead of decodes on a busy colocated GPU?
options: Neither, since prefill priority helps everyone
Throughput in tokens per second must drop
TTFT gets worse
TPOT/TBT gets worse: running streams stutter while new prompts are processed
explain: Prioritizing prefill keeps TTFT low but every prefill iteration delays the next token of every running request. Splitwise notes that letting a waiting prompt preempt token generation shortens TTFT but can substantially increase the tail of TBT. Throughput may even rise; latency of the other phase is what suffers.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: The KV handoff in detail: protocol, layouts and failures
question: Prefill runs TP=4 and decode TP=2 for a model with 8 KV heads and head-major KV blocks. For a 128-block request, how many block reads does each decode rank issue?
options: 128, one per block, as with equal TP
256: each D rank needs 4 heads held by 2 P ranks, so 2 reads per block
512: every D rank reads every P rank
64, because a D block holds two P blocks
explain: A D rank's 4 heads are split over 2 P ranks (2 heads each), so it reads 2 slices per block: 2 x 128 = 256. Reading every P rank would fetch heads the D rank does not own; block counts do not change with TP, only the heads per block slice.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: From sectors to partitions to image files
question: An MBR shows exactly one partition, type 0xEE, covering the whole disk. What should your tool do next?
options: Report a single unformatted partition
Read the GPT header at LBA 1 and its partition entries; the MBR is only a protective placeholder
Treat the disk as wiped, since 0xEE marks erased space
Search for 0x55 0xAA signatures to find hidden MBRs
explain: Type 0xEE is the GPT protective MBR. The real partition table is the GPT starting at LBA 1 (signature EFI PART). It does not mean unformatted or wiped.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: The USN change journal: a diary of every file change
question: The oldest record in a server's change journal is from three days ago. Your intrusion window starts two weeks ago. What do you write?
options: No files were changed before three days ago
The intruder deleted the journal
The journal does not cover the window; absence of earlier records says nothing about earlier activity
The server was rebuilt three days ago
explain: The journal is trimmed from the start once it exceeds its maximum size, so on a busy volume coverage is short. Deletion or a rebuild would need other evidence (for example a USN reset or a process event).

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: The registry in depth, and proving a USB drive was used
question: A registry key's last write time is 2026-03-02 14:28. Which statement is safe?
options: Every value under this key was written at 14:28
A user opened this key in regedit at 14:28
The key or at least one of its values was last modified at 14:28
The key was created at 14:28
explain: Microsoft defines it as the last time the key or any of its values was modified. It is per key, not per value, and it records modification, not viewing or creation.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Live acquisition and encryption: the Ross Ulbricht laptop (2013)
question: A live acquisition inevitably changes the running system. Which ACPO principle governs this?
options: Principle 1: no action should change data that may be relied on in court, so live acquisition is forbidden
Principle 3: only a second examiner may access live systems
Principle 4: the investigation lead must perform the acquisition
Principle 2: the person accessing original data must be competent and able to explain the relevance and implications of their actions
explain: Principle 2 covers the case where accessing original data is necessary. Principle 1 is the default, not a ban; Principle 3 requires an audit trail; Principle 4 puts overall responsibility on the person in charge.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: Why a billion vectors break in-memory graph indexes
question: Why does DiskANN keep PQ codes for every point in RAM instead of reading vectors from the SSD to compute distances during the search?
options: Each neighbor's distance would then cost its own random read, multiplying I/O by the degree
PQ distances are exact
The SSD cannot store full vectors
RAM is cheaper than SSD
explain: Search must score every neighbor of every expanded node, which is dozens of distance computations per hop. Fetching each neighbor's vector from SSD would be a random read per neighbor. Approximate PQ distances in RAM steer the search; exact vectors are only needed for the nodes actually read.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: CAGRA search on the GPU, and picking an index
question: A recommendation service sends one query at a time to a GPU CAGRA index, and the GPU is mostly idle. Which setting addresses this?
options: Multi-CTA search, which spreads one query across several thread blocks
A larger team_size
A smaller graph_degree
Single-CTA with a persistent kernel
explain: Single-CTA maps a query to one block, so a batch of 1 uses a sliver of the GPU. Multi-CTA assigns several CTAs to one query, each expanding a parent, which the paper designed for batch sizes of about 1 to 100. cuVS AUTO selects it for small batches.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: When preferences look certain: DPO overfits, IPO holds
question: Why does DPO's regularization fail on a pair that appears once in the data?
options: Because DPO forgets to load the reference model
Because the empirical preference for that pair is 1, and fitting probability 1 with a sigmoid needs an unbounded log-ratio gap regardless of beta
Because beta is too large by default
Because the gradient weight grows as the margin grows
explain: One label means the observed preference is 1. The logistic loss can always be lowered further by widening the gap, so the optimum sits at infinity and beta only changes the speed. The weight actually shrinks with the margin; that slows drift but never stops it.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Offline or on-policy: online DPO, and when RL still wins
question: In Tajwar et al.'s terms, what does DPO have and lack?
options: Has on-policy sampling, lacks a negative gradient
Has both
Has neither
Has a negative gradient, lacks on-policy sampling
explain: DPO explicitly pushes down the rejected answer's likelihood (a negative gradient) but trains on a fixed dataset, never sampling from the current policy. PPO and REINFORCE have both; SFT on chosen answers has neither.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Proving the new read path before trusting it
question: An experiment compared 20,000 reads with zero mismatches. The new path actually returns wrong data on 1 read in 100,000. How likely was this clean result?
options: About 1.8 percent
About 18 percent
About 50 percent
About 82 percent
explain: The probability of no mismatch is (1 - 0.00001) to the power 20,000, which is about 0.819. A clean run that short says little about rare bugs; you need roughly 300,000 comparisons for 95 percent confidence at this rate.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: The verifier: proving every path safe before it runs
question: A program loops `for i in 0..N` where N is read from a map value with no upper bound check. The verifier rejects it. Why?
options: Maps cannot be read inside loops
Loops are never allowed in eBPF
The verifier cannot prove the loop terminates within its limits, because N could be any 64-bit value
The JIT does not support loop instructions
explain: Bounded loops are allowed (since v5.3) only if the verifier can show the exit condition is reached within its 1M processed-instruction budget. An unbounded N defeats that proof. Clamping N to a small constant first fixes it.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: The three budgets a model must fit on a small device
question: A model has 250,000 int8 weights (244 KB) and its largest operator reads a 40 KB tensor and writes a 40 KB tensor. The target has 256 KB of flash and 64 KB of SRAM. What is the problem?
options: Nothing, both fit
The weights do not fit in flash
The peak activations (80 KB) do not fit in SRAM
The model must be fp32 to run on a CPU
explain: Weights live in flash: 244 KB is under 256 KB, though tight once code is added. Activations need the peak of input plus output, 80 KB, which is more than 64 KB of SRAM. You would shrink the largest feature map (fewer channels or lower resolution), not the weights.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Fewer operations and fewer weights, then shipping it
question: You replace every 3x3 conv in a model with depthwise separable blocks and the MAC count drops 8x, but measured latency on your phone CPU drops only 2x. Which explanation is most plausible?
options: The MAC formula is wrong
Depthwise layers do few MACs per byte moved, so they are limited by memory traffic and kernel efficiency rather than arithmetic
Separable convolutions use more parameters
Latency always scales exactly with MACs, so the measurement must be wrong
explain: MAC counts ignore memory traffic and kernel quality. A depthwise layer does only k x k MACs per input value, so it is often bound by memory bandwidth rather than arithmetic. This is why the pipeline ends with measurement on the device.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Pulse Secure and FortiOS, 2019: file reads that leaked passwords
question: An organisation patched its Pulse appliance in May 2019 and saw no alerts afterwards. In 2020 an attacker logs in through it as a real employee. What was missing?
options: A second firmware upgrade
Resetting every password that could have been read from the appliance before the patch, and requiring MFA
A reboot after patching
A stronger TLS cipher
explain: The patch stopped new file reads. Passwords already copied stayed valid until changed, and without MFA a password alone was enough to log in. This is exactly CISA's AA20-107A finding.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Exposure management: what you show the internet, continuously
question: Why combine an outside-in scan with the asset inventory instead of trusting either one alone?
options: The scan finds what is really exposed, including unknown devices; the inventory supplies owners and true versions. Each corrects the other
Scans are always more accurate than inventories
Inventories are required by law, scans are not
It makes the scan faster
explain: Equifax's scans missed a vulnerable system (prerequisite course), and inventories miss devices people set up without telling anyone. The join of the two is what produces actionable, owned findings.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Responding to a compromised appliance: evidence, rebuild, rotate
question: After a confirmed PAN-OS compromise, which item is most often forgotten in rotation?
options: The firewall's local admin password
The firewall's directory service account, which in Volexity's case was a domain admin
The firewall's hostname
The firewall's public IP address
explain: Admins remember the local admin password, but service accounts configured on appliances are easy to overlook because no person logs in with them. Volexity saw exactly such an account used to reach the domain controllers. Hostnames and addresses are not secrets.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Why RL makes reasoning long: the length bias in the policy loss
question: PPO with gamma = 1, lambda = 0.95 and value estimates near 0 sees a failed response (reward -0.5). Its per-token-averaged loss is about 0.099 at 100 tokens. About what is it at 1,000 tokens, and which way does that pull length?
options: About 0.010: the loss falls like 1/T, so longer failed responses are favored
About 0.99: the loss grows with T, so shorter responses are favored
About 0.099: GAE makes the loss independent of length
About -0.010: the sign flips once the response is long enough
explain: The leading term is $-R/(T(1-\lambda)) = 0.5/(T \times 0.05)$: 0.1 at T = 100 and 0.01 at T = 1,000 (exactly 0.0994 and 0.0100 in the code). A smaller loss for a longer failure is the pull toward length.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Budget forcing, effort levels and hard caps at inference
question: A request needs 4,800 reasoning tokens and a 400-token answer at its effort level. With max_output_tokens = 3,000 it fails; you retry at the same effort with the cap raised to 6,000. How many output tokens are billed in total for the two calls?
explain: The failed call bills its 3,000 reasoning tokens and returns no answer. The retry generates 4,800 + 400 = 5,200, all billed as output. Total 8,200. Lowering effort, not tightening the cap, is how you pay for fewer thinking tokens.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: HTML character references and the order a browser decodes
question: A filter rejects attributes whose text contains `javascript:`. Which attribute text gets past it but still produces a `javascript` scheme in the browser?
options: `https://a.example/javascript:`
`JAVASCRIPT:go()` after the filter lower-cases
`javascript:go()`
`javascript%3Ago()`
explain: The HTML parser turns `j` into `j` before the URL parser runs. The https URL only has `javascript:` in its path (and the filter blocks it anyway). A lower-casing filter catches `JAVASCRIPT:`. In `javascript%3Ago()`, `%3A` is not decoded when the scheme is parsed, so there is no `javascript:` scheme.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Lossy conversion: Windows Best-Fit and PHP CVE-2024-4577
question: In the toy, why does the check `arg.startswith("-")` miss the attack?
options: Python's `startswith` ignores invisible characters
The child process strips the first character
The soft hyphen is a dash in every encoding
The check runs on the wide string, and only the later ANSI conversion turns U+00AD into `-`
explain: At check time the first character is U+00AD, which is not `-`. Best-Fit mapping happens afterwards, on the way to the ANSI command line, so the check and the child see different strings.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: URL parser differentials: one URL, two hosts
question: Your redirect check uses Python's `urlsplit` and an exact host match; the browser follows the URL. Which input class is still most likely to cause a disagreement?
options: A plain `https://good.example/path`
URLs with a query string
URLs containing backslashes or control characters, which the URL Standard handles differently from many libraries
Upper-case scheme names like `HTTPS`
explain: Backslashes and control characters are exactly where WHATWG repair rules and other libraries diverge. Ordinary paths, queries and scheme case are handled the same by both.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Defender's checklist for encodings and parsers, and where to practise
question: A team fixes a reported bypass by adding the attacker's exact input to a blocklist. Why is that a weak response?
options: Blocklists are slow
Blocklists cannot hold Unicode
The underlying differential remains, so other spellings of the same meaning will still pass
It is a strong response if the list is reviewed monthly
explain: The bug is the disagreement between a check and a later reader. As long as it exists, an attacker can find another encoding, normalisation or parser quirk that produces the same effect.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: ETW: providers, sessions and consumers
question: A server's PowerShell Operational log has had no 4104 events for two days, while the same server shows normal process activity in Sysmon. What is the best first reading?
options: A possible logging gap or tampering worth checking, because silence from one source while others continue is itself a signal
Nothing happened: no one used PowerShell
Sysmon must be broken instead
4104 events are only written on domain controllers
explain: No PowerShell use for two days may be true, but a source going quiet while others continue is exactly how disabled providers or changed policies look. Check the logging policy and the provider state before concluding nothing happened.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: WMI: remote execution, event subscriptions and their telemetry
question: Sysmon logs events 19, 20 and 21 within a minute on a finance laptop, naming a CommandLineEventConsumer. What is this most likely to be?
options: Normal Windows Update activity
A user printing a document
Sysmon restarting after a crash
A permanent WMI event subscription being created: filter, consumer and binding, a known persistence technique (T1546.003)
explain: Events 19, 20 and 21 are filter, consumer and binding registration. Together, with a command-line consumer, they describe a full permanent subscription. Legitimate ones are rare on workstations, so investigate who created it.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Credential hardening: LAPS, LSA protection and Credential Guard
question: An intruder dumps the local Administrator hash on one LAPS-managed laptop. What does LAPS change about their next step?
options: Nothing, LAPS only protects domain accounts
LAPS deletes the local Administrator account
LAPS encrypts LSASS memory
The hash works only on that laptop, because every machine's local admin password is different, and it changes again on rotation
explain: LAPS gives each device a unique, rotated local admin password, so a hash from one machine does not authenticate to the others. It does not protect LSASS itself; that is LSA protection's and Credential Guard's job.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: XDR, MDR and running EDR well: the HSE lesson
question: At HSE, antivirus detected Cobalt Strike and Mimikatz on 31 March but nothing was blocked. According to the review, why?
options: The antivirus did not recognise either tool
The workstation was offline
Cobalt Strike disabled the antivirus first
It was set to monitor mode, so it recorded but did not block
explain: The PwC review, as summarised by Krebs, says the antivirus detected both tools but was set to monitor mode, so it did not block the malicious commands. Detection without blocking or response left the attacker six more weeks.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Scoring a disaggregation: MAE, NEP, NDE and F1
question: Two models have the same fridge MAE. Model A is off by 5 W on every sample; model B is exactly right except for a few samples off by a lot. Which metric separates them, and how?
options: NDE: B scores worse because squaring weights its few large errors more
F1: A scores lower because small offsets flip the on/off labels
NEP: A scores worse because it has more errors
None: equal MAE means every normalised metric is equal
explain: NEP is MAE times T divided by total energy, so equal MAE means equal NEP. NDE squares errors, so B's few large misses count more. F1 barely moves for A, since a 5 W offset on a 120 W fridge does not cross the 10 W on/off threshold.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Blocking: compare only pairs that could match
question: Adding a third rule, *same city*, to our toy blocking would do what?
options: Raise pairs completeness to 1.0 and keep the candidate count at 10
Recover r6-r7 (both Denver) but add many more pairs, lowering the reduction ratio
Have no effect, because city is not a name field
explain: City is low-cardinality (it has few distinct values): everyone in Austin would be paired with everyone else in Austin. It recovers r6-r7 but at a large cost in comparisons on real data. A stricter combined key (city plus name prefix of 2 letters, say) is the usual compromise.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Who runs the tenant: Entra roles, Global Administrator and PIM
question: A tenant has 3 Global Administrators, all eligible through PIM, but 14 users hold Application Administrator permanently, and one app they manage has the Graph permission RoleManagement.ReadWrite.Directory. What is the real number of paths to Global Administrator power?
options: 3: only the Global Administrators
0: PIM eligibility blocks all paths
14: but only if those users also hold Helpdesk Administrator
At least 17: any Application Administrator can add a credential to that app and use its permission to assign roles
explain: Microsoft's role reference warns that Application Administrators can add credentials to an app and act as it. An app with RoleManagement.ReadWrite.Directory can assign roles, so each of the 14 is a path, plus the 3 eligible admins.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Entra tokens: lifetimes, refresh tokens and revocation
question: A thief steals a refresh token issued to a mail client that Ana consented to for Mail.Read and Files.Read. What can the thief obtain?
options: Only mail access tokens, because the token was issued for Exchange
Nothing without Ana's MFA
Only an ID token
Access tokens for any resource the client was granted for Ana, including files
explain: Microsoft documents refresh tokens as bound to user and client, not to a resource. The client can redeem it for access tokens to any resource where it holds permission, and the MFA claim from Ana's original sign-in carries over.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Conditional Access in Entra: baselines and the gaps attackers use
question: A tenant's only Conditional Access policy requires MFA for 'All users' and excludes the group 'Service Accounts'. An attacker sprays passwords. Which account is the most valuable target?
options: A regular user, because MFA is optional for them
The emergency access account, because it has no MFA
A guest user
An account in 'Service Accounts': a correct password is enough, because no policy applies to it
explain: Excluded accounts are evaluated by no policy, so a sprayed password suffices. Emergency accounts should be protected by a phishing-resistant credential, not by Conditional Access; service accounts need managed identities or workload policies instead.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: A hardening baseline, an incident runbook, and where to practise
question: During an incident you find a malicious multitenant app with Mail.Read (application) in your tenant. What is the right first action on the app?
options: Delete the app's service principal
Reset the passwords of all users
Ask the app's publisher to delete the application object
Disable the service principal so it cannot obtain tokens or be consented to again, then remove its grants and investigate what it read
explain: Microsoft's consent playbook says to disable rather than delete: a deleted service principal can return when someone consents again, while a disabled one cannot get tokens. Then remove its grants and scope its access in the logs.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Level-triggered versus edge-triggered, and reading until EAGAIN
question: An ET server reads one 4096-byte chunk per event and then returns to epoll_wait. A client uploads 10,000 bytes in one burst and waits for a reply. What happens?
options: The server reads all 10,000 bytes over three wakeups
epoll_wait returns EAGAIN
The kernel splits the burst into three separate edge events
The server reads 4096 bytes and may never be woken for the remaining 5904, so the client hangs
explain: Once all the bytes are queued, nothing new arrives after the first 4096 are read, so there is no new edge, and epoll_wait can block forever with 5904 bytes in the buffer. This is exactly step 5 of the epoll(7) example. Fix: read until EAGAIN, or until a short read on a stream socket.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Split by query and keep a rotating sealed test set
question: Your team trains a learned reranker on click logs from January to June and evaluates on 300 labeled queries sampled from the same months. Which leak is most likely to inflate the test score?
options: The test queries use graded rather than binary labels
Many test queries, or close paraphrases of them, also appear in the training clicks
The test set is too large for a bootstrap confidence interval
The reranker uses a cross-encoder instead of a bi-encoder
explain: Popular queries repeat. A reranker trained on clicks for a query has effectively seen its answer. Split by query cluster and preferably by time (train on earlier months, test on later), so test queries are genuinely new. A 300-query set is not too large to bootstrap (lesson 4), and the reranker's design (a cross-encoder reads query and document together, a bi-encoder embeds each separately) does not create a leak.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Stack canaries: a tripwire in front of the return address
question: Why does the compiler insert the canary check just before `ret` rather than right after `strcpy`?
options: Because strcpy itself checks the canary
Because the return address is only used at ret, so checking just before it guards that use whatever code wrote to the frame
Because the check is free at ret but costly elsewhere
Because the canary is only written at the end of the function
explain: The canary protects the return address, and the return address is only consumed by ret. Checking just before ret covers every write that happened anywhere in the function body, not just one call. The cost is the same anywhere; strcpy knows nothing about canaries.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: RELRO, the GOT and FORTIFY_SOURCE
question: A binary is built with partial RELRO only. An attacker has a bug that writes 8 chosen bytes to a chosen address. Which table is still a useful target, and which flag closes it?
options: The stack canary; -fstack-protector-all
The PLT stubs; -Wl,-z,noexecstack
.got.plt, left writable for lazy binding; -Wl,-z,now (full RELRO)
.text; -fPIE
explain: Partial RELRO leaves .got.plt writable so lazy binding can fill it in. Adding -z now makes the loader resolve everything at start-up so the whole GOT can be made read-only.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Kernel mitigations: SMEP, SMAP, KASLR, KPTI and EternalBlue
question: According to Microsoft's analysis, which change made EternalBlue as leaked fail on the newest 64-bit Windows 10 even before patching?
options: The HAL region it relied on was no longer executable and its address was randomized
SMBv1 was removed from Windows 10
Windows 10 used stack canaries in the kernel
The NSA patched the exploit
explain: The exploit placed its payload in the HAL region at a known, executable address, which held on Windows 7. Windows 10 made that memory non-executable and the latest 64-bit builds randomized it. The SMBv1 bug itself remained until MS17-010 was applied.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Four independent counters that refuse to scale
question: Two threads write different fields of one struct that fits in a single cache line. A colleague says this cannot be slow because nothing is shared. What is the best reply?
options: Right, the compiler places each field on its own line automatically
Right, only atomic variables can cause cache contention
Wrong, but only because the struct needs a mutex
Wrong, the fields share one cache line, so each write forces the line to move between cores
explain: Compilers pack fields together to save space; they do not spread them across lines. Any write needs the whole line, so the two cores fight over it. No mutex is needed for correctness here, because the fields are distinct; the problem is purely performance.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: How big is a line, how to find false sharing, who pads
question: Why might a library avoid the C++17 constant `hardware_destructive_interference_size` in a public header?
options: Its value can change with compiler tuning flags, so separately built code may disagree on struct layout
It is not defined in C++17
It is always 64, which is too small
It only works with std::atomic members
explain: GCC sets it from -mtune, and its documentation warns that all translation units relying on it must use the same tuning. In a public header that is an ABI hazard, so libraries often use a fixed constant such as 128 instead.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Cheaper rounds and smarter servers: compression and FedOpt
question: On the skewed split with E = 5, a colleague replaces FedAvg with a well-tuned FedAdam and expects the toy to reach 2.3. Where does it converge, if it converges?
options: To 2.3, because adaptive steps correct client drift
To about 1.944, the same fixed point, because the averaged delta is zero there whatever the server does
To 1.667, the average of the local optima
It cannot converge, since Adam needs true gradients
explain: At 1.944 the clients' moves cancel in the weighted average, so the pseudo-gradient is zero and every server optimizer stops there. Server optimizers change speed and stability. To move the destination you must change what clients compute: less local work, a proximal term, or SCAFFOLD's control variates (lesson 5).

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Threats: what updates leak and how clients poison the model
question: An auditor argues that FedAvg's 5 local epochs per round make client updates safe to share in the clear. Based on the Inverting Gradients experiments, what is the best reply?
options: Correct: after 5 epochs the update no longer depends on individual examples
Correct only for convolutional networks
Wrong: 5 local epochs were no harder to invert than 1; only more images per update made reconstruction harder, and not safe
Wrong, because local epochs make updates larger and therefore easier to invert
explain: Geiping et al. found single-image reconstructions unimpeded even after 100 local steps, and their 8-image experiments were no harder at 5 epochs than at 1. Averaging over more images lowered quality, but some images from a batch of 100 were still recognizable. Formal protection needs differential privacy.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: ACORN-gamma: expand every neighbor list by gamma
question: Why does ACORN-gamma skip HNSW's RNG-based pruning when building neighbor lists?
options: It makes construction too slow
The pruned detour through a third node may fail the predicate, so the shortcut it relied on vanishes in the predicate subgraph
RNG pruning only works for cosine distance
HNSW never prunes at the bottom level
explain: HNSW drops edge v to b if some kept neighbor a is closer to b, trusting search to go v, a, b. For a predicate where v and b pass but a fails, that path does not exist. Without knowing predicates at build time you cannot prune safely, so ACORN keeps the near neighbors and uses a predicate-agnostic compression instead.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Fine-grained experts: split each expert into m slices
question: A team trains a small MoE at a modest budget and finds that $G = 16$ trains slower in wall-clock time than $G = 8$, though $G = 16$ has slightly lower loss per step. Which reading fits the scaling-law paper?
options: Granularity never helps; the law is wrong
Per-step loss keeps improving with $G$, but routing and small-matrix overhead grow with $G$, so the wall-clock optimum can sit at a lower $G$, especially for small models
$G = 16$ must have more active parameters
The loss improvement comes from more total parameters
explain: Finer experts keep active and total parameters fixed, so the per-step gain is real but diminishing. Krajewski et al. saw exactly this: at 64 x 7M, $G = 8$ beat $G = 16$ in wall-clock time because routing cost dominated. Higher $G$ pays off at larger budgets.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Putting it together: routing in DeepSeek-V3
question: A team copies V3's recipe but trains with very small global batches (a few sequences per step). Which risk grows most?
options: Future-token leakage from the bias
The shared expert stops training
Node-limited routing stops working
Per-step load imbalance, since batch-wise balancing cannot even out a batch that is mostly one domain, so busy experts stall the step
explain: The loss-free paper shows balance improving as the computation batch grows, and the V3 report lists imbalance within small batches as a challenge that large-scale expert and data parallelism (model copies each training on a different slice of the batch) solves. The bias uses only past batches, so there is no leakage.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: SPI flash, SMM and the write lock LoJax walked through
question: Why was RwDrv.sys useful to the LoJax operators?
options: It is a validly signed driver that gives low-level hardware access, so Windows loads it
It exploited a Windows kernel bug
It disables Secure Boot
It encrypts the SPI flash
explain: The driver belongs to a legitimate utility and carries a valid signature, so the kernel loads it. Its job is to read and write hardware registers, which is exactly the access a flash writer needs.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: The 2023 to 2026 Microsoft certificate rollover
question: A kiosk PC never received the 2023 certificates. What happens after the 2011 certificates expire in 2026, according to Microsoft?
options: It stops booting immediately
Secure Boot switches itself off
It keeps booting, but can no longer receive new boot manager, db, dbx and boot-level security updates
The TPM is cleared
explain: Expiry does not stop the existing chain from booting. The device simply falls off the update path, so future boot-level fixes never reach it.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Hardware roots of trust: Boot Guard, AMD PSB and Apple silicon
question: LoJax wrote a modified firmware image into SPI flash. On a machine with Intel Boot Guard in verified mode with the OEM key fused, what would most likely happen at the next boot?
options: Secure Boot would catch the new DXE driver
The ACM would find the firmware's initial boot block no longer verifies against the OEM key, and the policy would stop the boot
Nothing, Boot Guard only measures
The TPM would erase the implant
explain: ESET states that with Boot Guard available and properly configured, the machine would have refused to boot after the compromise. Secure Boot, which runs inside the modified firmware, would not.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Firmware updates, resilience and the BMC beside the CPU
question: A firmware update tool verifies the vendor's signature but accepts any signed version. Which NIST SP 800-147 recommendation does it miss?
options: Secure local update
Rollback prevention: refusing authentic but older images with known weaknesses
Non-bypassability
None
explain: 800-147 says the authenticated update mechanism should prevent rollback to an earlier authentic version with a known security weakness, for example by comparing version numbers.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-3: producer and consumer warps, then ping-pong
question: A teammate proposes giving the producer warpgroup as many registers as the consumers, "to be fair." What is the most likely effect?
options: Faster loads, because TMA needs registers for each byte copied
No effect, because register counts are fixed per kernel
Fewer registers for the consumers, forcing smaller tiles or spills in the math path
Better ping-pong, because both warpgroups can then do softmax
explain: TMA is issued by a single thread and copies data without staging it in registers. Registers given to the producer are taken from the consumers, which hold the accumulators; the paper deallocates producer registers and reallocates them to consumers for exactly this reason.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-4 backward, determinism and scheduling
question: A varlen inference batch contains short prefills followed by a few very long-context decodes. Which FlashAttention-4 scheduling idea addresses the resulting slowdown?
options: Conditional softmax rescaling
Sorting batches by their per-tile cost so the longest work starts first (LPT)
Emulating the exponential on FMA units
Switching to FP8
explain: This is load imbalance: if long work is processed last, a few SMs finish late while others sit idle. The paper launches a small preprocessing kernel to sort batches by cost and write a virtual-to-actual batch index map, which can be cached so sorting costs nothing on later calls.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Load-balanced scheduling, plan and run, and CUDA graphs
question: An engine calls plan() before every layer's run() in a 32-layer model. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, plan must precede every run
plan() must be called only once at startup
run() will use the wrong KV pages
It repeats identical CPU scheduling 32 times per step, since all layers share the same lengths
explain: The plan depends only on the sequence lengths and page arrays, which are the same for every layer in a step. The docs and paper design plan for reuse across all layers; calling it per layer adds CPU overhead to every step. Calling it only at startup is also wrong, because lengths change every step.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Generating data by following a velocity field from noise
question: Why was maximum-likelihood training of continuous normalizing flows expensive compared with flow matching?
options: The loss required simulating the ODE (and backpropagating through it) on every training step
The network had to output a full probability density instead of a velocity
Maximum likelihood cannot be used with Gaussian noise
It needed a discriminator network as in a GAN
explain: Likelihood training of a CNF integrates the ODE inside the training loop. Flow matching regresses the network onto a closed-form target velocity at a sampled point, so no simulation happens during training.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Relation to diffusion, and rectified flow in Stable Diffusion 3
question: Which statement best describes the relation between diffusion models and flow matching?
options: They are unrelated; diffusion requires an SDE and cannot be sampled with an ODE
Diffusion paths are Gaussian conditional paths within the flow matching framework, and diffusion models can be sampled with the probability flow ODE
Flow matching is a special case of DDPM with a different noise schedule
Flow matching can only learn straight paths, diffusion can learn curved ones
explain: Lipman et al. recover VE and VP diffusion paths as Gaussian conditional paths, and Song et al.'s probability flow ODE gives diffusion models a deterministic sampler. The marginal flow of any of these, including OT paths, can be curved.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Inductive invariants: from bounded checks to every N
question: In the TLAPS proof, which assumption lets the same proof cover 3, 5 or 1,001 acceptors?
options: AllowRestart = FALSE
Any two quorums intersect
Values has exactly two elements
TypeOK
explain: Step <1>3 needs one acceptor in both quorums, and QuorumsMeet supplies it for any size. NoRestart is needed too, but it is about the environment, not the size. The proof never mentions how many acceptors or values exist.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Ghost permissions, VerusSync and what a proof trusts
question: A Verus project verifies cleanly, yet in production the service corrupts data. Which explanation is NOT possible if Verus and Z3 are sound?
options: The top-level ensures clause did not state the property that matters
The verified exec function returned a value violating its ensures clause on some input
A trusted spec of an external crate was wrong
The code contains assume(...) that is false
explain: If the tools are sound and nothing false is assumed, every verified function satisfies its ensures on every input. Failures come from what was assumed or trusted, or from specs that say the wrong thing.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Fine-grained FP8 at scale: tiles, blocks and FP32 promotion
question: An FP8 GEMM with K = 8192 shows growing error versus a BF16 reference, even though inputs are well scaled. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The scales are stale; switch to delayed scaling
Too few mantissa bits in the inputs; switch all inputs to E5M2
Limited-precision accumulation inside the tensor cores; promote partial sums to FP32 every N_C elements
The output is BF16; write it in FP8 instead
explain: The DeepSeek report traces large-K error to about 14-bit accumulation in Hopper FP8 tensor cores and fixes it by moving partial sums to FP32 on CUDA cores every 128 elements. E5M2 inputs would make precision worse, not better.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: NVFP4: 16-value blocks, E4M3 scales and a tensor scale
question: A tensor has amax 10. One block's amax is 0.05. What is that block's ideal scale before E4M3 rounding, in the stored (multiplied) form?
options: 448, like every block
explain: First s_enc = 6 x 448 / 10 = 268.8. The block's decode scale is 0.05 / 6 = 0.00833, and the stored value is 0.00833 x 268.8 = 2.24, comfortably inside E4M3's range. Without the tensor scale, 0.0083 would sit in E4M3's subnormal region.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Abuse economics: make every attempt cost more than it earns
